comparedAgainst: https://ronjeffries.com/xprog/articles/acsbowling/ — Ron Jeffries' 2003 "Adventures in C#: The Bowling Game", the canonical worked kata the article itself cites. Fetched: Jeffries' test order (Hookup, GutterBalls, Threes/AllOnes-equivalent, Spare, Spare2, Strike, StrikeFinalFrame, SpareFinalFrame, Perfect, alternating strike/spare) and his implementation are both materially different from this article's — Jeffries builds polymorphic `Frame` subclasses (`OpenFrame`/`SpareFrame`/`StrikeFrame`/`BonusRoll`) each holding a reference to the shared throws list and computing its own score via `FirstBonusBall()`/`SecondBonusBall()`/`FrameSize()`, whereas this article uses a flat `List<int> rolls` walked by a single `rollIndex` pointer with `IsStrike`/`IsSpare` predicate methods and no Frame type at all. Confirms the article's own claim ("written fresh for this article, not taken from that or any other published solution") rather than contradicting it. Jeffries' piece is also purely narrative code-and-prose, no captured tool output.

https://codingdojo.org/kata/Bowling/ — a widely-used, language-agnostic kata brief for the same exercise. Fetched: it states the rules and test cases in scoresheet notation (X, /, -) with no code in any language and no captured compiler or test-runner output at all; it is a problem statement, not a worked walkthrough. Against both comparisons, this article's differentiator holds up: every intermediate step, including the ones that are supposed to fail, is a real compiled/run program with byte-for-byte captured xUnit output (assembly name, Total/Failed counts, actual exception text), which neither comparison source has.

https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html — fetched. The article's quoted definition ('a technique for building software that guides software development by writing tests') and the Beck/late-1990s/Extreme-Programming attribution match the source verbatim.

https://martinfowler.com/articles/is-tdd-dead/ — fetched. All three quotes the article attributes to this page check out verbatim: Beck on JUnit's 'clear interfaces that make a sweet spot for TDD'; Fowler on payroll calculations vs. html rendering; Heinemeier Hansson's note that TDD in an MVC web app is harder than clean PHP.

https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/canon-tdd — fetched twice (once for the five-step structure, once specifically for 'Fake It'/'Obvious Implementation' terminology). The five-step structure the article describes (test list, one test, make it pass, refactor if needed, repeat/cross off) matches the source. 'Fake It' and 'Obvious Implementation' are NOT in this source — see issues below.

https://xunit.net/docs/getting-started/v3/getting-started — fetched. Confirms the in-process runner distinction the article cites: v3 test assemblies are 'stand-alone executables that can be directly run' and discover/execute/report inside that same process, contrasted with the separate-process console runner — matches the article's paraphrase.
justification: `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/test-driven-development.md` from PowerShell, run 4 times back to back: PASS, blocks=23, executed=12 every time, no flakiness. I independently re-derived the bowling scoring algorithm by hand rather than trusting the article's narration. The final Score()/FrameScore() logic (check strike first: score += 10 + rolls[i+1] + rolls[i+2], advance 1; else spare: score += 10 + rolls[i+2], advance 2; else open: score += rolls[i]+rolls[i+1], advance 2; fixed 10-frame outer loop) is the textbook-correct rollIndex-pointer bowling algorithm. I hand-traced all five scenarios against it: gutter game (20 zeros) = 0; all-ones (20 ones) = 20; spare+3 (5,5,3,17×0) = 10+3 for frame 1, +3 for frame 2, +0×8 = 16; strike+3+4 (10,3,4,16×0) = 10+3+4 for frame 1, +3+4 for frame 2, +0×8 = 24; and the perfect game (12×10) frame-by-frame: each of the first nine frames adds 10+10+10=30 (running total 270 after frame index 8), the tenth frame (rollIndex=9) adds 10+rolls[10]+rolls[11]=30 for a final 300, with the last array access at index 11 in a 12-element list — no out-of-bounds anywhere. All five match the article's claimed outputs and the captured `text output` blocks. I then re-traced each red step by hand: Lap 1's `new Game()` with no `Game` class is a genuine CS0246 (the harness itself enforces the diagnostic code, not just prose); Lap 2's all-ones test against `Score() => rolls.Sum()` genuinely returns 0 instead of 20 (Sum of twenty 1s... wait, correctly 20 ones sum to 20, but the red block still has `Score() => 0` hard-coded from Lap 1, so it genuinely returns 0, matching 'Actual: 0'); Lap 3's red step (`Sum()` on 5,5,3,17×0) genuinely sums to 5+5+3=13, matching 'Actual: 13' exactly; Lap 4's red step, run against the pre-strike-branch code, hits `IsSpare(18)` on a 19-element array (indices 0-18) and reads `rolls[19]`, which is genuinely out of range — confirmed by index arithmetic, not just trusted from the output text — matching the captured `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. The perfect-game checkpoint's `Game` class (Lap 5) is byte-for-byte identical to Lap 4's `Game` class (same fields, same IsStrike/IsSpare, same Score body) — the 'no new code' claim is literally true, only a new `[Fact]` was appended. The buggy `while (rollIndex < rolls.Count)` variant: I traced all five tests independently. GutterGame, AllOnes and SpareThenThree all use exactly 20 rolls and the pointer lands on exactly 20 after 10 frames' worth of advances, so the loop condition `rollIndex < 20` correctly stops with no extra iteration; StrikeThenThreeFour uses 19 rolls and the pointer lands on exactly 19 for the same reason. Only AllStrikes (12 rolls) diverges: after 10 strike-frames the pointer sits at 10, and 10 < 12 is true, so the loop runs an eleventh 'frame,' finds a strike at index 10, and needs `rolls[10+2]=rolls[12]` in a 12-element list (valid indices 0-11) — genuinely out of range, and it is specifically and only the AllStrikes test that crashes, matching the captured output exactly (`Total: 5, ... Failed: 1`, `AllStrikes_ScoresThreeHundred [FAIL]`, the same `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`). The refactor lap's `FrameScore(int rollIndex, out int ballsUsed)` is a pure mechanical extraction of the same three branches with the same arithmetic and the same advance amounts (1 for strike, 2 for spare/open) — no behavior change, and the five tests it's checked against are the same five, still green. Sourcing: every fetched citation (Fowler's TDD bliki, all three quotes from Is TDD Dead?, Canon TDD's five-step structure, xUnit's in-process-runner description) matches the article's paraphrase or quotation exactly. Jeffries' 2003 kata is real and current at the cited URL, and its polymorphic Frame-subclass design is different enough from this article's flat-array/rollIndex design that the article's 'written fresh... not taken from that or any other published solution' claim holds up under direct comparison, not just on the writer's word. The self-reported corrections are reflected correctly: the article never claims 12 rolls is any kind of maximum (it only says a perfect game takes 12 rolls, fewer than a strike-free game's 20, which is true and properly scoped), and there is no 'gets actively skipped' claim anywhere in the text. The 'when TDD helps/hurts' section is genuinely reasoned from the sourced Beck/Fowler/Heinemeier-Hansson debate (stable-contract logic vs. exploratory-interface code), not cheerleading — it states a rule of thumb and immediately scopes it ('not a universal one'). Against the two kata references I could independently fetch (Jeffries' narrative walkthrough, CodingDojo's language-agnostic brief), this article's differentiator is real: every step, including the ones staged to fail, is a compiled-and-run program with exact captured runner output, which neither comparison source has. The one thing keeping this off a higher score: the article attributes 'Fake It' and 'Obvious Implementation' by name to Beck in two places, but the only Beck source in front matter (Canon TDD) does not use either term — I fetched it a second time specifically to check and it isn't there. The terms are real (from Beck's 2002 book Test-Driven Development: By Example) and the definitions given are accurate, so this is not a factual error, but per the Editorial Brief's sourcing rule ('every non-obvious factual claim has a primary source, fetched and read during research... cite inline where the claim is made'), naming a specific person's specific named technique without that source in front matter or an inline citation is a gap, not a nit.

The article's only Beck source in front matter, Canon TDD, does not use either term (confirmed by fetching it specifically to check) and no other source for the attribution is listed or cited inline. The definitions given for both terms are accurate, so this is not a factual error, but it is an uncited non-obvious claim under the Editorial Brief's sourcing rule.

issues.problem: Traced by hand: after the fixed 10-frame outer loop is replaced with `while (rollIndex < rolls.Count)`, the buggy variant's loop condition (rollIndex=10, count=12) technically permits up to two more passes (rollIndex 10, then 11), but execution never reaches a second pass — the first extra pass itself throws when it evaluates `rolls[rollIndex+2]` = `rolls[12]`. The phrase is defensible as describing what the loop condition allows rather than what actually executes, but as written it can read as two completed reads.
issues.fixLooksLike: Tighten to something like "the loop's guard would allow up to two more passes ... the first of which reaches past the end of the list" to avoid implying two reads happen before the crash.
